articles.title: Building a Webhook-Driven Agent: Async Patterns for Slow Enterprise APIs
articles.excerpt: Most agent demos call an API and wait. That works until the API is an ERP that takes 40 seconds to answer, or a batch endpoint that takes ten minutes. Then the agent hangs, the request times out, a re…
articles.body: Most agent demos call an API and wait. That works until the API is an ERP that takes 40 seconds to answer, or a batch endpoint that takes ten minutes. Then the agent hangs, the request times out, a retry fires, and now you've created the same purchase order twice. This post walks through the pattern I reach for instead: accept the task, hand the slow work to a queue, let the ERP call us back, and keep a polling job around for the days the callback never arrives. The code is Python with FastAPI and httpx. The ERP API is made up, so adapt the field names to yours. Why synchronous waiting breaks There are three problems with waiting inside the agent's request: Timeouts. Load balancers and clients give up long before a slow system finishes. Retries without protection.

articles.body: There is a category of device that never appears in your observability stack: the wall clock. It draws 12 watts, it has an IP address, and nobody ever checks whether it's right. Which is a strange thing to say about a device whose only function is being right. Last quarter I ended up responsible for 34 of them across three buildings — 8-inch LED seven-segment displays, HH:MM:SS, purchased as NTP synchronized clocks. This post is the unglamorous story of making them observable, including the two things I got wrong.

articles.title: Claude Code in a monorepo: how to split CLAUDE.md files across teams
articles.excerpt: A single CLAUDE.md file works well for one team in one repository. In a monorepo it slowly turns into a problem. The payments team adds its rules, the frontend team adds theirs, the platform team adds…
articles.body: A single CLAUDE.md file works well for one team in one repository. In a monorepo it slowly turns into a problem. The payments team adds its rules, the frontend team adds theirs, the platform team adds a deployment section, and soon every session starts by loading three hundred lines of instructions, most of which have nothing to do with the task. That costs more than context space. The Claude Code documentation recommends keeping each CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, because longer files consume more context and reduce how reliably Claude follows them. It also warns that when two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. A file that four teams edit is where contradictions come from.

articles.title: PowerShell Get-ChildItem -Filter vs -Include: The Real Difference (and Why -Include Returns Nothing)
articles.excerpt: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\logs -Include *.log looks correct, runs without an error, and returns nothing. Swap -Include for -Filter and the files show up. Same cmdlet, same pattern, different result. The…
articles.body: Get-ChildItem -Path C:\logs -Include *.log looks correct, runs without an error, and returns nothing. Swap -Include for -Filter and the files show up. Same cmdlet, same pattern, different result. The two parameters run at different stages. -Filter goes to the provider, which skips non-matching files while it enumerates. -Include and -Exclude run inside PowerShell after the provider has already returned items, and only under certain path conditions. Once you know which stage you're working with, the "returns nothing" bug and the slow scripts both make sense. Every command below was run in PowerShell 7.4.6 on Linux. I point out where Windows or Windows PowerShell 5.1 behaves differently, based on Microsoft's docs, because I couldn't test those here. Build a small lab Run this once.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
articles.excerpt: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's…
articles.body: On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad - whether it's a still image, video, audio, or text - that "has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence" to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants' ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad … Read the full story at The Verge.

articles.body: On Episode 233 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and guest host Rick Jenet are joined by Dr. Amanda Smith-Hackler, the Director of Education for the Universities Space Research Association and Principal Investigator for the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) Scholars and STEM Workforce Development Programs, about the new and exciting opportunities available to young people seeking to enter the space workforce.
